title: Why People With Half Your Talent Seem to Keep Winning
author: Evans, Ethan
summary: Ethan Evans and Jason P. Yoong address the frustrating career experience of watching less-skilled colleagues advance faster. Their argument: talent is necessary but not sufficient -- visibility, advocacy, and manager alignment are what convert hard work into promotions. The article identifies concrete patterns that high-talent but low-visibility professionals fall into: doing excellent work in isolation, assuming results speak for themselves, and failing to build the relationships that generate sponsorship. Evans draws on his Amazon experience to argue that the career advancement system rewards those who manage upward as skillfully as they execute. The piece provides a practical framework for becoming more visible without compromising integrity: proactively sharing wins, aligning with manager priorities, and building advocates who will speak on your behalf in promotion discussions.
points: Talent is necessary but not sufficient: career advancement requires visibility, advocacy, and manager alignment -- not just strong performance.
Results rarely speak for themselves in large organizations: work done in isolation, however excellent, cannot generate sponsorship from people who don't know about it.
Manager alignment is the highest-leverage career activity: understanding what your manager is measured on and delivering against those priorities is the single most reliable path to promotion.
Building advocates is a proactive discipline: sponsors who argue for you in promotion discussions are built through consistent relationship investment, not assumed to emerge naturally.
Upward communication is a skill, not self-promotion: regularly sharing progress and framing your contributions in terms of team and business outcomes are professional competencies.
quotes: The uncomfortable truth about career growth: talent is not enough -- visibility, advocacy, and manager alignment turn hard work into promotion.
Two people can do identical work. One gets promoted. The other gets stuck wondering why. The difference is rarely effort. It's almost always visibility and advocacy.
Your manager cannot advocate for what they do not know. Keeping your head down and delivering excellent results is a strategy that works only if someone is watching.
The people who seem to win with half your talent have figured out that careers are built at the intersection of competence and connection.
This is not about politics. It's about understanding how decisions get made and ensuring that the people who make them have accurate information about your contributions.
